patient_name: Director of nursing interview — adapting to US patient-care culture
chief_complaint: Answer a US director of nursing's questions on patient refusal, speaking up to physicians, interpreters, and patient autonomy versus family decision-making

team_brief.title: Job interview: cultural adaptation — refusal, hierarchy, interpreters, and autonomy
team_brief.patient: Interview: Registered Nurse (adult medical unit), US urban safety-net hospital
team_brief.location: Final-round video interview; you are the candidate, and Maria Castellano, director of nursing for medicine, leads the questions
team_brief.situation: Your clinical background has already been checked. This interview is about how you will adapt to US patient-care culture: a very diverse patient population, direct communication with physicians, language access, and patient autonomy. The director has hired many international nurses and asks open, sometimes uncomfortable, scenario questions.
background: You have 5 years of experience on an internal medicine ward in a Seoul tertiary hospital, including many oncology patients.
You passed the NCLEX-RN in 2025 and hold a US RN license. Your English is strong, but you have a noticeable accent.

In your hospital, nurses rarely questioned a physician's order directly and usually went through the head nurse; families often heard a serious diagnosis before the patient and decided whether the patient should be told.
When patients did not speak Korean, you sometimes relied on a family member or a phone translation app.
key_data: The hospital serves a very diverse urban population; about a third of patients prefer a language other than English, and qualified medical interpreters are available 24/7 in person, by video, or by phone.

Hospital policy: a competent adult patient makes their own decisions and controls who receives their health information; family members, friends, and especially children are not used as interpreters except in an emergency.

The hospital uses TeamSTEPPS: any staff member can raise a safety concern with the 'CUS' words (Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue) and use the chain of command. A pharmacist is available 24/7 for medication questions.
When a patient asks for a different nurse, the charge nurse decides how to respond under hospital policy; the patient's care must continue safely in the meantime.
team_brief.your_request: Show the director that you can adapt your practice to US expectations of patient autonomy, speaking up, and language access, while staying calm, respectful, and safe.
must_include: A calm, professional response to a patient who refuses your care: keep the patient safe, involve the charge nurse, and do not argue or take it personally.
How you would speak up to a physician about an order you believe is unsafe — directly, with facts, and escalating through the chain of command if needed.
Choosing a qualified medical interpreter over a family member, and how you communicate through one (speak to the patient, short sentences, teach-back).
Respecting a competent adult patient's right to know and decide, even when the family asks you to withhold information — while acknowledging the family's intentions.
Honest reflection on how practice in Korea differs and what you are doing to adapt.

kickoff_text: Hi, thanks for making the time today. I'm Maria Castellano, director of nursing for medicine. We've looked at your clinical background, so today I really want to hear how you'd work here. Let's jump in — how do you think nursing here will be different from what you're used to in Korea?
persona_override: You are Maria Castellano, director of nursing for the medicine service at a large US urban safety-net hospital, running a final-round video interview with an internationally educated RN. You are warm but searching; you ask open questions and let silence sit. You have hired many international nurses, and your real concern is not their clinical skill but whether they will speak up to physicians and respect patient autonomy in a US setting — a previous hire gave a dose she doubted because 'the doctor said so'. Ground truth about the hospital: diverse urban population; about a third of patients prefer a language other than English; qualified interpreters 24/7 in person, video, or phone; policy says competent adults make their own decisions and control who gets their information, and family or children are not used as interpreters except in an emergency; TeamSTEPPS with CUS words and a chain of command (charge nurse, then house supervisor, then the attending physician or medical director); requests for a different nurse go to the charge nurse, who decides under hospital policy; ethics consultation and palliative care teams are available; a pharmacist is available 24/7 for medication questions; international nurses get a 12-week orientation and a peer mentor. Ask these questions one at a time, in order: (1) 'How do you think nursing here will be different from what you're used to in Korea?' (2) 'You walk into a patient's room and he says he doesn't want a foreign nurse — he wants someone else. What do you do?' (3) 'A physician orders a dose you believe is too high. You call him, and he's short with you and says just give it. What do you do?' (4) 'Your patient speaks only Spanish. Her son says he'll translate so you don't have to wait for the interpreter. How do you handle that?' (5) 'A Korean-American family asks you not to tell their mother she has cancer — they say someone from your culture will understand. What do you do?' Probing rules: if an answer is only general ('I would respect everyone'), ask 'What would you actually say to him?' or 'Can you give me an example from your own experience?' For question 2, if they say they would simply leave, ask 'And who's looking after him in the meantime?'; if they say they would convince him they are qualified, ask 'And if he still says no?' For question 3, if they would give the dose, ask 'Talk me through that — you still think it's too high?'; if they go only to the charge nurse, ask 'Would you say anything more to the physician yourself?'; if they hold the dose, ask 'And then what?' For question 4, if they accept the son, ask 'Any concerns with that?' For question 5, if they agree to keep the secret, ask 'What if she asks you directly whether she has cancer?'; if they would simply tell her, ask 'And how do you handle the son and daughter?' If the candidate says 'we' throughout a personal example, ask 'What did YOU do?' Use at most two probes per question. Never reveal what the 'right' answer is, never say an answer was good or bad, never coach — use neutral acknowledgements only ('Okay', 'Mm-hm', 'Thank you'). After question 5, say 'Those are my questions — what would you like to ask me?' and answer briefly from the ground truth. Then thank them, say the recruiter will contact them with the decision, and close. Keep your turns short — one to three sentences.
learning_objectives: respond to a patient who refuses your care by keeping the patient safe and involving the charge nurse
speak up to a physician with 'I'm concerned' and hold a dose you believe is unsafe until it is clarified
use the chain of command when a safety concern is not resolved
use a qualified medical interpreter instead of a family member and speak directly to the patient
respect patient autonomy by asking the patient how much she wants to know
reflect honestly on differences between nursing in Korea and the US
suggested_questions: I'd stay calm and not take it personally. I'd make sure he was safe and had what he needed right then, and I'd let the charge nurse know straight away so she could decide how to cover his care.

I'd tell him, 'I'm concerned about this dose — it's higher than the usual range, and I'm not comfortable giving it until we clarify it.' If he still insisted, I'd hold it and go up the chain of command, starting with my charge nurse.

I'd thank her son, but explain that hospital policy is to use a medical interpreter so his mother gets accurate information and he can just be her son. Then I'd call the interpreter line and speak directly to her.

In Korea families often decide what the patient hears, so this is something I've had to think about. Here I'd acknowledge that the family wants to protect her, and involve the physician so someone can ask her how much she wants to know and who she wants involved.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Adapting to US nursing culture: patient refusal of a nurse, speaking up across hierarchy, interpreter use, and patient autonomy
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in AHRQ TeamSTEPPS (CUS and the two-challenge rule), the US National CLAS Standards on language access, and general US principles of informed consent and patient privacy; hospital policy and state law apply
core_concepts: In the US, each nurse is accountable for every medication they give; 'the physician ordered it' does not remove that responsibility, so an order believed to be unsafe is clarified before it is given.
TeamSTEPPS gives nurses scripted tools to cross hierarchy: CUS ('I'm concerned... I'm uncomfortable... this is a safety issue'), the two-challenge rule, and the chain of command.

US hospitals are expected — under federal civil-rights rules, accreditation standards, and their own policies — to provide meaningful language access, usually through qualified medical interpreters rather than family members.
Before or while questioning a dose, the nurse can check a drug reference and ask the pharmacist, so the concern is backed by facts.

A competent adult patient has the right to information about their own condition and to make their own decisions; a respectful approach asks the patient how much they want to know and whom they want involved, rather than overriding the family or deceiving the patient.
Interviewers value honest reflection on cultural differences and a concrete plan to adapt more than claims that there will be no difficulty.
diagnostic_clues: Questions framed around conflict ('he's short with you and says just give it') test whether the candidate will advocate for the patient under pressure.
A family member offering to interpret is a common, well-meant shortcut that the interviewer expects the candidate to decline politely.
A family appealing to shared culture ('you will understand') tests whether the candidate separates personal background from professional obligations.
common_misconceptions: If the physician insists on the order, legal responsibility passes to the physician.
Questioning a physician is disrespectful, so the nurse should only ever go through the charge nurse.
A bilingual family member is just as good as a professional interpreter, and faster.
Respecting Korean culture means agreeing to hide a diagnosis from the patient.
A patient who refuses a nurse because of their background must either be argued with or simply left.
dangerous_errors: Giving a medication the nurse believes is unsafe because the physician said to.
Lying to a patient who asks directly about their diagnosis, or promising the family that the patient will never be told.
Using a child or family member to interpret consent, discharge teaching, or a serious conversation when a qualified interpreter is available.
Walking away from a patient who refuses care without arranging for someone else to take over.
Sharing a competent patient's information with family members the patient has not authorized.
management_principles: Patient safety first in every scenario, then escalate through the right person: charge nurse, physician, chain of command.
Speak up with facts (checked against a drug reference or with the pharmacist) and a clear request ('I need this clarified before I give it'), and document the conversation per policy.
Through an interpreter: speak to the patient in the first person, use short sentences, and confirm understanding with teach-back.
Acknowledge the family's protective intentions, involve the physician, and let the patient set how much they want to know; consider ethics or palliative care support.
boundaries_and_exceptions: How hospitals respond to patient requests for a different caregiver based on the caregiver's background varies by policy and is a leadership decision, not one the nurse makes alone.
Disclosing a new serious diagnosis is normally the physician's role; the nurse supports, answers within scope, and escalates the patient's questions.
Emergency situations may justify an ad hoc interpreter briefly until a qualified interpreter is available; local policy and state law apply.
Federal language-access rules and guidance have changed over time; the hospital's current interpreter policy is what the nurse follows.
This scenario practises interview communication; it is not legal or ethics advice.
